newsitem.title: USA: IBM preparing employee buyout program.
newsitem.headline: IBM preparing employee buyout program.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp is preparing to offer a voluntary employee buyout plan to a few thousand eligible employees, in a move to rebalance its worldwide workforce, sources and analysts said.

The computer giant, which is seeing huge growth in its services business, is seeking more skilled employees in its growth areas but does not need the skills of some employees in the slower growth areas, such as its maintenance business, analysts said. The offer is expected to come this week.
A spokesman for the Armonk, N.Y.-based computer maker declined to comment.

The New York Times reported that IBM is considering offering a buyout plan to 3,000 to 5,000 eligible employees. But one industry source said that IBM is trying to "flush out" between 6,000 to 10,000 employees from some areas of its business, such as maintenance and its European operations, while it adds in its fast growing computer services business.
IBM is adding employees to its services operations and has already added 10,000 employees to services, with plans to add 4,000 to 5,000 more during the remainder of 1996.
At the end of 1995, IBM had a total worldwide workforce of 225,000, with 110,000 of those employees in the U.S.

An IBM spokesman said that IBM expects its total U.S. employment to grow in 1996, but he would not give any specific numbers. Analysts said that IBM hopes its offer is accepted by some employees in European countries such as Italy, where local laws make it very difficult to lay off employees.

"What would make sense is for them to reduce the workforce overseas, particularly in Europe," said Bob Djurdjevic, president of Annex Research in Phoenix. "It's much more expensive to do it there and it's much more advantageous for people to leave."
Maintenance, or availability services, is another area.

While the buyout plan and other possible inducements have not been announced yet, some industry sources said that the plan under consideration may require that employees have been at IBM for at least five years.

The plan could involve employees accepting the offer receiving a certain amount of pay for every year of service at IBM, with a maximum ceiling on the amount of time. Employees may also be offered a retraining program worth in excess of $2,000 each and a transitional medical plan.
"Some people with critical skills will not be eligible," said one source. "The goal is to rebalance skills across IBM."

"IBM is re-engineering itself to the new paradigm called the Internet and services...and skills are required to enter this new world," said Sam Albert, a Scarsdale, N.Y.-based consultant. "IBM is becoming leaner and meaner but in order to be meaner they have to have the right skills."

Analysts do not expect IBM to have to take a restructuring charge for the move, because it said in its second quarter conference call that it has set aside $400 million for remaining restructuring moves in the second half of this year.
But if a certain number of employees did not accept the offer, IBM might have to consider layoffs, analysts said.

Some analysts said that IBM has been having a hard time getting some employees to accept its severance packages and that as one measure, it had even considered raising the age at which IBM employees can retire with benefits from the present 55.
One analyst who asked not to be named said it was possible that IBM has now dropped this idea.

"There have been several things that have been considered, but nothing has been implemented," said another source, adding that if IBM changed its retirement plan, many IBMers in their mid 50s who already are of retirement age and fully vested might have more of an incentive to leave.
